[1] rewrite

```
- **Why the limit on the gap between runs with different time steps is 0.5%.**
  No record says how it was chosen. It dates from an earlier, approximate
  method, whose runs differed by about 0.04% in the alveolar concentration and
  by more in mixed venous. Besides the 0.5% limit, the test requires each gap
  between two runs to stay below 1e-14 as a fraction. Any gap that breaks 0.5%
  is at least 1e-8, so it breaks 1e-14 too. Today the 0.5% limit changes no
  outcome.
```

[2] rewrite

```
- **How to change it.** A fork with an approximate method fails 1e-14 even
  when its arithmetic is correct. For example, a first-order method shows gaps
  near 1.4e-11. Relax 1e-14, and 0.5% becomes the working check. Set it above
  the method's own gaps at the time steps the test uses, and below a difference
  that a learner could see. The constants are in
  `tests/reference/test_sevo_patient.py`.
```

[3] rewrite

```
**The release check on the time step, and why it allows a 0.5% difference.** The
model advances in fixed steps of 0.1 s, and a shorter step should give almost the
same result. Before each release, a test reruns the first minute of the default
sevoflurane induction with steps of 0.1 s, 0.05 s and 0.025 s. Each run's
alveolar, vessel-rich and mixed-venous concentrations must be within 0.5% of the
run with the next shorter step. A compartment that holds almost no agent also
passes if its two values differ by less than 0.000001 vol%, because there a tiny
difference is a large percentage. The 0.5% was set for the simulator's earlier
calculation method, at about ten times the 0.04% alveolar difference that method
showed. The current method's runs agree to better than one part in a trillion
(simulated 2026-10-03), so the much tighter limits in the paragraphs above are
the ones that would catch a real error.
```

[4] rewrite

```
The 5e-3 relative tolerance was chosen when the simulator used an earlier
calculation method (an operator split). That method showed a relative gap of
4e-4 in the alveolar fraction between steps of 0.1 s and 0.025 s, and 5e-3 is
about ten times that gap. The tolerance is kept as a coarse check, because with
the current, exact method the same comparison gives relative gaps of about
1.4e-13 (simulated 2026-10-03). For a fraction so close to zero that a relative
gap means little, the 1e-8 absolute tolerance lets a negligible difference pass.
```

[5] rewrite

```
**The release check on the time step, and why it allows a 0.5% difference.** The
simulator moves the model forward in fixed time steps, normally 0.1 s long. A
shorter step should give almost the same result. If it does not, the step is too
long. Before each release, a test runs the first minute of the default
sevoflurane induction three times, with steps of 0.1 s, 0.05 s and 0.025 s. In
each run, the alveolar, vessel-rich and mixed-venous concentrations must be
within 0.5% of the run with the next shorter step. The check compares each run
only with the next shorter step. A compartment that still holds almost no agent
also passes if its two values differ by less than 0.000001 vol%, which is one
part in a hundred million of the gas. There, a tiny difference can be a large
percentage, so a percentage means little. With the current calculation method,
the three runs agree to better than one part in a trillion (simulated
2026-10-03), so this check is now only a coarse safety net. The much tighter
limit in the paragraphs above is the one that would catch a real error.

The 0.5% limit was set for the simulator's earlier calculation method. That
method's 0.1 s and 0.025 s runs differed by about 0.04% in alveolar
concentration, so the limit allowed about ten times that difference. Under that
method, a direct comparison of those two runs would have failed, because their
mixed-venous concentrations differed by 0.55%. At one minute, those
concentrations have barely begun to rise.
```

[6] rewrite

```
**The three agents' maximum dial settings come from two classes of vaporizer.** The sevoflurane
and isoflurane maxima are those of variable-bypass dials. Desflurane's is the top of the Tec 6's
range, and a Tec 6 is a heated gas–vapour blender. The model fixes ambient pressure at 760 mmHg
(§ "Assumptions"). At that pressure, the same dial setting on either class gives the same partial
pressure, so the model does not need to know which class a limit came from. The classes would
differ only at reduced ambient pressure, which is not modelled (§ "Known limitations").
```
